source: The eight shared exercises, in the shape of the Greek shared file. Answer strings that the Latin exercise fixes are copied exactly. German has four cases, so the case and government items use the case names.

pos.note: Der points out the king. German has a definite article, and Latin has none.
Das points out the book. The article agrees with Buch, which is neuter and singular.
König names the king, and it is the subject of spricht.
Buch names the book, and it is the object of sieht.
Spricht says what the king does. It is the present, third person singular, of sprechen.
Sieht says what the woman does. It is the present, third person singular, of sehen.
Gute tells what sort of king, and it takes the weak ending after der.

pos.orig: The woman sees a good book.
pos.note: Gutes tells what sort of book. After ein, a neuter singular adjective takes the mixed ending.
Oft tells how often he speaks. An adverb keeps one form.
Gern modifies kommt. An adverb keeps one form.

pos.orig: The king comes into the city.
pos.note: In joins kommt to the place. For the place to which, in takes the accusative.

pos.orig: The woman comes with the king.
pos.note: Mit joins kommt to the person who comes along. Mit takes the dative.

pos.orig: The king and the woman speak.
pos.note: Und joins the two subjects. A conjunction keeps one form.

pos.s: Der König spricht, aber die Frau kommt.
pos.orig: The king speaks, but the woman comes.
pos.note: Aber joins the two clauses. A conjunction keeps one form.
Ich stands for the speaker, and it is the subject of sehe.
Mich stands for the person seen. It is the accusative of ich, and no noun follows it.
Gesprochen is the past participle of sprechen. With hat it makes the Perfekt.

pos.orig: The woman has seen the book.
pos.note: Gesehen is the past participle of sehen. With hat it makes the Perfekt.
Ach is a cry, and it stands outside the clause. Duden prints Ach as an interjection.
Oh is a cry, and it stands outside the clause. Duden prints o(h) and Oh.

decline.q: Is the marked word declinable or indeclinable?
decline.a: Declinable: a noun, which takes endings
ds: Declinable: a verb, which takes endings
Declinable: an adjective, which takes degrees
Declinable: a pronoun, which still shows case
Indeclinable: an adverb, which keeps one form
decline.why: König is a noun. It takes an ending for the genitive singular, Königs, and another for the plural, Könige.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: König is the subject of spricht. The subject stands in the nominative, and the article is der.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Frau is the subject of kommt. The subject stands in the nominative, and the article is die.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Ich is the subject of sehe. The subject pronoun stands in the nominative. The accusative is mich.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Menschen is the object of sieht. The article is den, and the weak noun adds -n in the accusative singular.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Mann is the object of sieht. The noun keeps the spelling of the nominative. The article den marks the accusative. Latin would change the noun.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Buch is the object of sieht. A neuter noun has one spelling for the nominative and the accusative, as in Latin. The verb shows that this Buch is the object.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Mannes marks the owner of the book. That is the genitive. Duden prints des Mann[e]s, and the sentence uses Mannes.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Frau marks the owner of the book. That is the genitive. The same spelling der Frau is also the dative, and here there is no verb that would make Frau an indirect object.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Freundes marks the owner of the book. Duden prints des Freundes as a genitive singular of Freund.

cases.s: Der König gibt dem Mann das Buch.
cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Mann is the person who receives the book. Geben takes a dative for the receiver and an accusative for the thing given. The article dem marks the dative, and the noun keeps its singular spelling.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Königen is the dative plural. Mit takes the dative, and the ending -n is the one Duden prints in den Königen.

cases.q: What case is the marked word?
cases.why: Für takes the accusative. The article den marks that case, and König itself does not change.

govern.why: Für takes the accusative. Duden calls für a preposition with the accusative. The article is den.
Ohne takes the accusative. The Duden example is ohne jeden Zweifel. The article here is den.
Gegen takes the accusative. Duden says the preposition gegen governs the accusative.
Mit takes the dative. Duden names mit among the prepositions that require the dative. The article is dem.
Statt takes the genitive in standard written German. Duden names statt among the genitive prepositions. The form is des Freundes.

Wegen takes the genitive in standard written German. The noun here shows the genitive ending. The bare singular that stays uninflected, as in wegen Umbau, is a different pattern, and it is not this sentence.

govern.q: What case does in take for the place to which?
govern.why: In takes the accusative for the place to which. The Duden question is wohin, and the printed example is in die Stadt. The article die is that accusative.

govern.q: What case does in take for the place where?
govern.why: In takes the dative for the place where. The Duden question is wo, and the printed example is im Haus. Der Stadt is the same dative, written without the contraction.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: König is masculine and singular, and the case is nominative. After der the weak ending is -e, so gute agrees.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Frau is feminine and singular. After eine the mixed ending is -e, so kleine agrees. The phrase is nominative or accusative, and both of those cells are kleine.

agree.a: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
ds: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Buch is neuter and singular. With no article the strong ending for the nominative or the accusative is -es, so gutes agrees.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Frau is feminine. Gutes is the strong neuter singular, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Both words are singular.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: König is masculine. Kleines is the strong neuter singular, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Both words are singular. The strong masculine nominative is kleiner.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Stadt is feminine. Kleines is the strong neuter singular, so the adjective disagrees in gender. Both words are singular.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Bücher is plural. Gutes is singular, and the strong nominative plural is gute, so the number does not agree. Both words are neuter.

ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
agree.why: Meere is plural. Gutes is singular, so the number does not agree. Both words are neuter.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: Königs is genitive. Gutem is the strong dative, so the case does not agree. Both words are masculine and singular. The strong genitive is guten Königs.

agree.a: Faulty: the adjective does not agree in case
ds: Sound: the adjective agrees with its noun
agree.why: Mannes is genitive. Kleinem is the strong dative, so the case does not agree. Both words are masculine and singular. The strong genitive is kleinen Mannes.

produce.why: The genitive singular of König is Königs. Duden prints des Königs, and no second spelling.
The dative plural of Buch is Büchern. Duden prints den Büchern. The nominative plural is Bücher.
The nominative plural of Stadt is Städte. The accusative plural and the genitive plural have the same spelling. The dative plural is Städten.

The accusative singular of the weak noun Mensch is Menschen. The same spelling is the dative singular, the genitive singular, and every plural case. The cell asked is the accusative singular. The nominative singular is Mensch.
The nominative plural of Garten is Gärten. The plural already ends in -n, so the dative plural has the same spelling.
The dative plural of Pferd is Pferden. Duden prints den Pferden.
The dative plural of König is Königen. Duden prints den Königen.
The genitive singular of Garten is Gartens. Duden prints des Gartens, and no second spelling.
With no article, the strong neuter nominative of gut is gutes. The same spelling is the strong neuter accusative. The cell asked is the nominative.
Seid is the present, second person plural, of sein. The third person plural is sind.
Sein takes sein in the Perfekt. The third person singular is ist gewesen.
Hat is the present, third person singular, of haben. The stem drops b. The second person singular is hast.
Hättest is the Konjunktiv II, second person singular, of haben. Duden prints that one spelling. The Präteritum of the same person is hattest.
Wird is the present, third person singular, of werden. The second person singular is wirst.
Würdest is the Konjunktiv II, second person singular, of werden. The Präteritum of the same person is wurdest. The older wardst is not this cell.
Machen takes haben. The third person singular of the Perfekt is hat gemacht. The participle is gemacht.
Spricht is the present, third person singular, of sprechen. The vowel is i. The second person singular is sprichst.
Spräche is the Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of sprechen. The first person singular has the same spelling. The Präteritum is sprach.
Gab is the Präteritum, third person singular, of geben. The first person singular has the same spelling. The present is gibt.
Kommen takes sein. The third person singular of the Perfekt is ist gekommen. The participle is gekommen.
Siehst is the present, second person singular, of sehen. The third person singular is sieht.

Sähe is the Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of sehen. The first person singular has the same spelling. The Präteritum is sah. Duden also prints sähest and sähst for the second person, and those are not this cell.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The article fits the noun, and the noun and the verb fit. A finite verb makes the sentence complete.

cong.s: Die Frau hat das Buch gesehen.
cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The parts fit, and the Perfekt is a finite verb, so the sentence is complete. Whether she has in fact seen the book is not asked.

cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Die agrees with Pferde, and sind gekommen agrees with that plural subject. Kommen takes sein. The sentence is complete.

cong.s: Der König hat dem Mann das Buch gegeben.
cong.a: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
ds: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: The subject, the dative, the accusative, and the Perfekt of geben fit. A finite verb finishes the sentence.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Gute fits König, and der fits König. There is no verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Kleine fits Frau, and eine fits Frau. There is no verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
cong.why: Das fits Buch, and des Mannes is a genitive. There is no finite verb, so the sense is not yet complete.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: König is singular. Sprechen is the plural form, and the same spelling is the infinitive. Neither fits this subject. Sprechen is a real form, and the fault is the join.

cong.a: Incongruous: the parts do not fit with one another, so the construction fails
ds: Complete: the parts fit, and the sentence is finished
Congruous: the parts fit, but the sense is unfinished
cong.why: Frau is feminine and das is neuter. The parts do not fit. Each word is a German form, and the fault is the join.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form German does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Sprichte is not a form of sprechen. The present, third person singular, is spricht. The fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form German does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Büchers is not the plural of Buch. The plural is Bücher. Sind is a real form, and the fault is in the one noun.

vices.a: Barbarism: a form German does not have
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Geseht is not the participle of sehen. The participle is gesehen. Hat is a real form, and the fault is in the one word.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Der and guter are both real forms. After der the adjective takes the weak ending, which is gute. The fault is the join.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Bist is a real present of sein, the second person singular. The subject Frau is third person singular, so the verb does not fit it. The third person is ist.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Den is a real masculine accusative, and Frau is a real feminine noun. The accusative feminine is die. The fault is the join.

vices.a: Solecism: good forms are badly joined
ds: No fault: the sentence is sound
A figure: the poets are allowed this departure
vices.why: Mit and den are both real forms. Mit takes the dative, which is dem. Den is accusative. The fault is the join.
